title: Fixture: Playing Closed Positions
blurb: A one-module test course exercising all three question kinds and an interleaved illustration. Not shipped content.

principle.markdown: Closed positions are not "stall and pray". They have concrete plans: **maneuver** your worst piece to its best square, **restrict** the opponent, create a **second weakness**, and **time the pawn break**. When you feel you can only shuffle, you have stopped naming a plan — not run out of them.
principle.remember: A locked position is a plan you haven't named yet, not the absence of one.

illustrations.source: Standard opening theory (Ruy Lopez, Morphy Defence); move-score is public fact, annotations original (clean-room, spec 227).

focus.text: After ...a6 White must decide the fate of the bishop. Retreating keeps the pin's pressure alive rather than trading it off.

ask.prompt: White to move. Keep the tension in this closed-ish setup — where does the bishop go?
ask.explain: Bxc6 hands Black the bishop pair and half-opens the b-file for free; it relieves the very tension you want to keep. Ba4 retains the pin's latent pressure and keeps the plan alive.

focus.text: White castles first — safety before the maneuvering begins. No break is timed yet; the pieces come out before the pawns commit.

questions.prompt: You feel you can 'only find moves that stall'. What has actually happened?
options: The position is objectively drawn and there is nothing to do.
You have stopped naming a concrete plan, not run out of them.
You must immediately force a pawn break to create chances.
questions.explain: 'Nothing to do' is the feeling, not the position. The mistake is abandoning plan-selection: closed positions still offer maneuver, restriction, a second weakness, and a timed break. Forcing a break now (option 3) is the opposite error — rushing before the pieces are ready.

questions.prompt: Black just played ...a6, attacking the bishop. Keep the tension — play the move.
questions.explain: Ba4 is the mainline: it keeps the pin's pressure and the slow-build plan. Bxc6 (the Exchange Variation) is also playable but concedes the bishop pair — accepted here, but understand you have traded tension for a structural bet, not stalled.

questions.prompt: In your own words: name a concrete plan for White in this quiet Ruy Lopez, and say what makes it a plan rather than 'shuffling'.
questions.modelAnswer: A plan names a target and a route: e.g. complete development (O-O, Re1, c3, d4), then maneuver the b1-knight via d2-f1-g3 toward the kingside/centre while restricting Black's ...d5 break. The common mistake is treating the quiet as emptiness and pushing a premature break (an early d4 or f4) before the pieces support it — that creates weaknesses instead of pressure.
rubric: Names a concrete target or square, not just 'improve position'.
Includes a piece route or pawn break, not only defence.
Distinguishes purposeful maneuvering from aimless shuffling.
Avoids advocating a premature break before development finishes.
